CITATION:

Alshawwa v Kalo
, 2026 MBPC 15

THE PROVINCIAL COURT OF MANITOBA

BETWEEN:

Fadel
Alshawwa                      )                  E. Dolcetti

)                  for
F. Alshawwa

)

-and-                                        )

)

)

Michael
Kalo                            )                  M. Kalo

)                  appearing
on his own behalf

)

)

)

)

)                  Reasons
for Decision

)                  Delivered
Orally: February 27, 2026

)                  Hearing
Held: February 3, 2026

(citations omitted orally)

TRASK JJP

Summary:
The defendant has
made various preliminary motions. In summary: I – the defendant’s recusal
motion is denied; II – the defendant’s application for a publication ban is
dismissed; III – the defendant has been provided with clear instructions on
serving the applicant and filing materials for this matter; IV – the
defendant’s motion to strike the present proceedings for amounting to
relitigating a previously decided matter is denied; V – the defendant’s motion
to replace sheriff officers with private security in the courtroom is
dismissed;  VI – the defendant’s motion to bring a service animal is granted,
on conditions; and VII – the defendant’s application for a stay of proceedings
pending an appeal on the recusal decision is denied. A reminder about
appropriate courtroom decorum is also set out and a caution about possible
consequences should that not occur.

Introduction

[
1
]

Mr. Alshawwa has applied for what is
commonly referred to as a “peace bond,” being a recognizance order, against Mr.
Kalo through
section 810
the
Criminal Code of Canada
, RSC 1985 (the
Code)
.
The recognizance hearing was initially set for February 3, 2026. Mr. Kalo made
an application for an adjournment on that date, and it was granted (
see
Alshawwa
v Kalo
,
2026 MBPC 14
for more).

[
2
]

Following the adjournment decision, Mr.
Kalo proceeded to bring various preliminary motions. Despite advising the Court
that he would file written applications should his adjournment request be
granted, Mr. Kalo proceeded to launch directly into his various preliminary
motions and indicated that he was doing so out of respect for the Court’s time.
Some of the motions and applications brought were somewhat unclear, and some
Mr. Kalo later said he was abandoning only to then refer to them later. No
filings were made regarding the applications or motions, and all the
applications or motions were supported only by oral arguments, apart from some
exhibits. There were few if any references to case law or legislation in the
arguments on the applications. I informed the parties of my decisions regarding
some of those motions with brief reasons, and I reserved on others. I indicated
full reasons would follow on the next appearance date. These are those reasons.

Issues

[
3
]

Mr. Kalo brought various motions, and I
will consider each in turn. First, he made a motion for recusal. Second, he
applied for a publication ban. Third, he sought clear instructions on how the
defendant is to serve the applicant and/or the applicant’s counsel. Fourth, he
made a motion to strike. Fifth, Mr. Kalo applied for replacement courtroom
security. Sixth, he made a motion to bring a service animal to the subsequent
hearings. Lastly, though not in the chronological order of how it came before
the Court, Mr. Kalo stated he would be seeking to appeal the decisions on the
recusal application, should it not be made in his favour, prior to the
substantive hearing on the peace bond itself, and would be seeking a stay of
proceedings for that purpose.

I – Motion for Recusal

The Defendant’s Motion

[
4
]

Mr. Kalo made a motion that I recuse
myself. The basis for this motion was somewhat unclear. Beyond simply applying
for my recusal, Mr. Kalo took the position that “all judges of this court”
should be recused from hearing this matter. He grounded his motion on two
aspects: who the applicant is and who the defendant is.

[
5
]

Mr. Kalo raised concerns that the
applicant/informant is a sheriff at the Winnipeg Law Courts Building, which is
the same Court hearing the applicant’s application. He argued that the
applicant being represented by a lawyer from the Government of Manitoba’s Civil
Legal Services branch emphasizes this concern. He did not expand on this further.

[
6
]

Mr. Kalo went on to claim that at least
eleven judges of the Manitoba Provincial Court are tainted by concerns of
actual bias where he is concerned. He reviewed his dealings with several judges
in some detail, including an alleged past intimate relationship with one Provincial
Court judge, complaints he has made to the Minister of Justice about various
judges, things he has said to relatives of sitting judges that could cause
offence, amongst other claims. He referenced being the subject matter of many
articles, including in the Jewish Post, that amount to an attack on his
character, which he believes at least some judges will have read or heard about
or subscribed to. Mr. Kalo claimed that the judges he named as affected by
concerns of actual bias may use their power to influence their sister or
brother judges, or to direct a judicial justice of peace under them.

[
7
]

To address his concerns, Mr. Kalo proposed
that a higher court justice or a judge from a different province, perhaps via
Zoom, ought to preside. Mr. Kalo noted that he was unsure of the Court’s
jurisdiction to make such an order.

[
8
]

After prompting as to whether Mr. Kalo had
specific concerns in my regard, Mr. Kalo asked me the nature of my relationship
with Brandon Trask. Without providing this information, I asked Mr. Kalo to
clarify the nature of his concerns before determining the appropriate next
steps. He said simply that he has had “dealings” with Brandon Trask. When asked
for details of those dealings, Mr. Kalo expressed reluctance – first abandoning
that line of argument and then later, when pressed, clarifying that they are
“not pillow buddies.” He said that their relationship has been professional in
nature and he noted that he has observed Brandon Trask in the media. When I
asked how that relationship could give rise to a reasonable apprehension of
bias, Mr. Kalo said that Brandon Trask knows him as a serious man and he is
concerned that this hearing could result in Mr. Kalo later being treated differently.

The Applicant’s Response

[
9
]

Counsel for the applicant referenced
Yukon
Francophone School Board, Education Area #23 v Yukon (Attorney General),

2015 SCC 25
,
[2015] 2 SCR 282
(“
Yukon Francophone School Board
”) for the
test on reasonable apprehension of bias, and she noted that there is a strong
presumption of judicial impartiality that is difficult to displace.

The Law, Analysis and Decision

[
10
]

Yukon Francophone School Board
is
the leading Supreme Court decision on reasonable apprehension of bias. Abella
J, writing for the Court, set out the following:

[20]
The test for a reasonable apprehension of bias is undisputed and was first
articulated by this Court as follows:

. . .
what would an informed person, viewing the matter realistically and practically
— and having thought the matter through — conclude. Would he think that it is
more likely than not that [the decision-maker], whether consciously or
unconsciously, would not decide fairly. [Citation omitted.]

(
Committee
for Justice and Liberty v. National Energy Board
,
1976 CanLII 2 (SCC)
,
[1978] 1 S.C.R. 369
, at
p. 394,
per de Grandpré J. (dissenting))

[21]
This test — what would a reasonable, informed person think — has consistently
been endorsed and clarified by this Court…

[22]
The objective of the test is to ensure not only the reality, but the
appearance

of a fair adjudicative process. The issue of bias is thus inextricably linked
to the need for impartiality. In
Valente
, Le Dain J. connected the dots
from an absence of bias to impartiality, concluding “[i]mpartiality refers to a
state of mind or attitude of the tribunal in relation to the issues and the
parties in a particular case” and “connotes absence of bias, actual or
perceived”: p. 685. Impartiality and the absence of the bias have developed as
both legal and ethical requirements. Judges are required — and expected — to
approach every case with impartiality and an open mind: see
S. (R.D.)
,
at para. 49, per L’Heureux-Dubé and McLachlin JJ.

[23]
In
Wewaykum
, this Court confirmed the requirement of impartial
adjudication for maintaining public confidence in the ability of a judge to be
genuinely open:

. . .
public confidence in our legal system is rooted in the fundamental belief that
those who adjudicate in law must always do so without bias or prejudice and
must be perceived to do so.

The
essence of impartiality lies in the requirement of the judge to approach the
case to be adjudicated with an open mind.
[Emphasis added;
paras. 57-58.]

[24]
Or, as Jeremy Webber observed, “impartiality is a cardinal virtue in a judge.
For adjudication to be accepted, litigants must have confidence that the judge
is not influenced by irrelevant considerations to favour one side or the
other”: “The Limits to Judges’ Free Speech: A Comment on the Report of the
Committee of Investigation into the Conduct of the Hon. Mr Justice Berger”
(1984), 29
McGill L.J.
369, at p. 389.

[25]
Because there is a strong presumption of judicial impartiality that is not easily
displaced (
Cojocaru v. British Columbia Women’s Hospital and Health Centre
,

2013 SCC 30
,
[2013] 2 S.C.R. 357
, at para.
22
), the test for a reasonable
apprehension of bias requires a “real likelihood or probability of bias” and
that a judge’s individual comments during a trial not be seen in isolation: see

Arsenault-Cameron v. Prince Edward Island
,
1999 CanLII 641 (SCC)
,
[1999] 3 S.C.R. 851
, at para.

2
;
S. (R.D.)
, at para. 134, per Cory J.

[
11
]

In
Wewaykum Indian Band v Canada
,

2003 SCC 45
,
[2003] 2 SCR 259
, the Court noted that:

…it is
worth repeating that the standard refers to an apprehension of bias that rests
on
serious grounds
, in light of the strong presumption of judicial
impartiality.  In this respect, de Grandpré J. added these words to the now
classical expression of the reasonable apprehension standard:

The
grounds for this apprehension must, however, be substantial, and I . . .
refus[e] to accept the suggestion that the test be related to the “very
sensitive or scrupulous conscience”. (
Committee for Justice and Liberty v.
National Energy Board
,
supra
, at p. 395)

[See
paragraph 76; emphasis added.]

[
12
]

The Court further set out that considering
a reasonable apprehension of bias claim:

… is an
inquiry that remains highly fact-specific.  In
Man O’War Station Ltd. v. Auckland
City Council (Judgment No. 1)
,
[2002] 3 N.Z.L.R. 577
,
[2002] UKPC 28
, at
par. 11
, Lord Steyn stated that “This is a corner of the law in which the
context, and the particular circumstances, are of supreme importance.”  As a
result, it cannot be addressed through peremptory rules, and contrary to what
was submitted during oral argument, there are no “textbook” instances. Whether
the facts, as established, point to financial or personal interest of the
decision-maker; present or past link with a party, counsel or judge; earlier
participation or knowledge of the litigation; or expression of views and
activities, they must be addressed carefully in light of the entire context.
There are no shortcuts.

[See
paragraph 77.]

[
13
]

While I recognize that the applicant in
this matter is a sheriff at the Winnipeg Law Courts Building, where this matter
is to be heard and where I also work, I am not able to conclude that that alone
would make a reasonable, informed person, viewing the situation realistically,
think it is more likely than not that I will not decide the matter fairly,
consciously or unconsciously. There is nothing suggesting I have a connection
in any way to the applicant, nor am I aware of any such connection. That a
lawyer from Civil Legal Services is representing the applicant, based on his
employment relationship as a sheriff working for the province of Manitoba, does
little to change that – government lawyers appear in court regularly and there
is no presumption of partiality for the government or Crown, and, again, there
is nothing to suggest I have any personal connection with counsel or her office
that would affect my ability to decide this matter fairly.

[
14
]

That Mr. Kalo has concerns there is a real
risk that judges of this Court are biased against him must similarly be dismissed.
Even if I simply accept the claims Mr. Kalo has made regarding particular
judges of this Court – which I do not – he has not established that an informed
person would conclude it is more likely than not that I would not decide the
matter fairly. This line of argument lacks specificity and appears to be based
on an unfounded claim of undue influence by numerous Provincial Court judges –
toward their brother and sister judges and in relation to judicial justices of
the peace. Whether or not Mr. Kalo has made out that certain Provincial Court
judges ought not to hear his matters is frankly not for me to consider – I am to
consider whether Mr. Kalo has established a reasonable apprehension of bias in
my regard.

[
15
]

As a judicial justice of the peace, I have
taken an oath of allegiance and an oath of office, as required by section 59 of

The Provincial Court Act
, CCSM cC275, which mirrors the oath every judge
of the Provincial Court makes. Krahn ACJ, as she then was, has noted that:

[34]      The
Provincial Court of Manitoba is composed of two sets of judicial officers:
provincial court judges and judicial justices of the peace. Both are imbued
with judicial independence and appointed pursuant to the
Provincial Court
Act
…

[
See
R
v Eisbrenner
,
2019 MBPC 3
, at para
34
.]

[
16
]

It has been established that “the
threshold for a successful allegation of perceived judicial bias is high,” and
that the presumption that judges will dutifully fulfill their oaths of office
“can be displaced with ‘cogent evidence’ that demonstrates that something the
judge has done gives rise to a reasonable apprehension of bias” (see
R v
S(RD)
,
1997 CanLII 324 (SCC)
,
[1997] 3 SCR 484
at para
117
). No such cogent evidence has been
presented in this case. The presumption of my judicial independence and
impartiality has not been displaced by a bald assertion of improper influence
by other judicial actors or by my association to the same Provincial Court as
judges Mr. Kalo claims are or may be biased against him.

[
17
]

Mr. Kalo appears to be hinting at the combination
of the applicant being a sheriff at the Law Courts, Civil Legal Services representing
the applicant on this matter, and his concerns about potential for real bias
from Provincial Court judges creating a conspiracy against him. He made various
disjointed outbursts throughout the hearing on February 3, 2026, about the
courts and Counsel for the applicant’s office being controlled by “Jewish
masters,” telling the Court to “follow the trail of money. They’re long-nosed,
greedy, entitled, spoiled brat [sic], corrupt, perverted Jews that control [Counsel
for the applicant’s] office,” “Jewish masters control this court … and the
justice system,” and referring to the Court as a “kangaroo court,” amongst many
other things. Insofar as Mr. Kalo is alleging a broader conspiracy, there is again
no cogent evidence to support these assertions and they are categorically dismissed.
While I will come back to appropriate courtroom decorum and conduct at the end
of this decision, I will reiterate now, as I did in the course of the hearing
on February 3, 2026, that many of Mr. Kalo’s outbursts were utterly
inappropriate in a court of law – both for the hateful and despicable content of
what he said and the manner in which he persisted in interrupting, yelling, and
generally disrupting the proceedings.

[
18
]

Mr. Kalo has also indicated that my
potential relationship to Brandon Trask is also a basis for his reasonable
apprehension of bias claim. While I recognize that in some circumstances it may
be incumbent on me to provide information about my associations or
relationships, I am satisfied based on the nature of the relationship that Mr.
Kalo has claimed to have with Brandon Trask that it is neither necessary nor
appropriate for me to do so in this case. Mr. Kalo has claimed to have a “professional
relationship” with Brandon Trask through a rights clinic, and he has stated
that he knows him through the media, which I take to mean he has observed Brandon
Trask in the media. Mr. Kalo has denied having a personal or intimate
relationship with Brandon Trask. He has not indicated he is a client of Brandon
Trask’s or that he has a business relationship or otherwise with him. Mr. Kalo
said he has respect for Brandon Trask, that Brandon Trask has seen him as a
serious person, and that he’s concerned these proceedings may change how
Brandon Trask views him.

[
19
]

I fail to see how Mr. Kalo having had professional
dealings with Brandon Trask, or having seen him in the media, without more, could
possibly rise to the level that an informed person would conclude it is more
likely than not a decision-maker would not decide this matter fairly,
regardless of the unstated nature of my relationship or association to Brandon
Trask. Mr. Kalo appears to be concerned about the potential for reputational
harm to himself flowing from these proceedings; as such, I would remind Mr.
Kalo that these applications and the peace bond hearing itself take place in
open court and are public proceedings.

[
20
]

In all, I am dismissing Mr. Kalo’s recusal
motion as I am not satisfied that a reasonable apprehension of bias has been
established.

II – Publication Ban

The Defendant’s Motion

[
21
]

In requesting a publication ban on these
proceedings, Mr. Kalo argued that he deserves protection to his reputation and
he noted that “too many people’s reputations might be hurt,” presumably if no
such order were made. He did not expand on this. He broadly referred to his
children and pointed to the potential for tension between Israeli and
Palestinian communities in Winnipeg to increase because of these proceedings.
He stated that “Hamas terrorists can be very dangerous,” and noted that the applicant
“is a terrorist… from Gaza,” but then immediately denied having called the
applicant a terrorist, as the applicant alleges in the particulars to this
matter.

[
22
]

After making innumerable comments of a
sexual nature about a judge of this Court, despite many warnings to keep to
appropriate and relevant comments about the proceedings, Mr. Kalo also indicated
that this hearing “has to do with the secret, intimate life of a Jewish judge”
and “out of concern for her reputation,” he was seeking a publication ban, in
the interest of ensuring intimate details would not be made public beyond what
is necessary. Mr. Kalo did not explain how his sexual references to this judge
and their alleged intimacy relate in any way to the recognizance order sought
by the applicant.

[
23
]

Further, Mr. Kalo did not identify this
Court’s authority to make such an order as he requested.

The Applicant’s Response

[
24
]

Counsel for the applicant advised that she
was unsure of the Court’s authority or jurisdiction to order a publication ban
in this context. She noted further that she has learned that Mr. Kalo has
already sent emails to the media regarding these proceedings.

The Law, Analysis and Decision

[
25
]

Most of the publication bans permitted under
the
Code
would appear to have no application to the within matter. While
there is an Information before the Court for this matter, there are no charges
or offences at issue. Further, I have heard nothing to suggest that restricting
the publication of the identity of certain victims or witnesses would be in the
interest of the proper administration of justice (see s. 486.5(1)).

[
26
]

I cannot see how the judge Mr. Kalo has
persistently named and discussed in a sexual manner during the proceedings
could amount to a victim or witness on the matter before the Court in which the
applicant is seeking a recognizance order against Mr. Kalo. I am cognizant that
many of the comments Mr. Kalo made during the proceedings were universally offensive
and rude, and some of his outbursts unquestionably amount to sexual harassment,
or inappropriate sexual commentary and intimidation, all of which formed the
basis of various warnings by this Court. These comments had no bearing on the
substantive matter before the Court or on Mr. Kalo’s various applications. While
these comments and outbursts may cause both offence and harm to the individuals
they related to, they are extraneous to the matter at hand.

[
27
]

Mr. Kalo has said that without a
publication ban, tensions could increase between the Israeli and Palestinian
communities in Winnipeg, however a publication ban at most would restrict the
publication of the identities of witnesses or victims – it would not be a full
prohibition on publication of the proceedings.

[
28
]

I am not of the opinion that such an order
would be in the interest of the proper administration of justice. Instead, I am
satisfied that the proper administration of justice weighs in favour of no
order being made to restrict the identity/identities of victims or witnesses in
this case. Maintaining the open court principle is essential. I consistently
addressed Mr. Kalo’s comportment toward the Court and justice system
participants, along with many vile allegations and outrageous comments he made
during the proceedings on February 3, 2026. Insofar as Mr. Kalo is concerned
about reputational harm that may come to him from these proceedings, I would
remind him that he is responsible for his behaviour.

III – Service by the Defendant

[
29
]

Mr. Kalo sought clarification on how to
serve the applicant for these proceedings.

[
30
]

Counsel for the applicant advised that Mr.
Kalo has been provided with her work address and instructed not to attend in
person but to send any materials by mail. She suggested that, given the nature
of the recognizance order being sought by the applicant, who works at the
Winnipeg Law Courts Building, Mr. Kalo notify Sheriff Services before attending
the Court.

[
31
]

Given the level of vitriol Mr. Kalo
leveled against counsel during the proceedings on February 3, 2026, including
comments of a sexual nature, I approved counsel for the applicant’s proposed
methods of service. Similarly, noting the degree of commotion that Mr. Kalo created
during the proceedings, I indicated it was appropriate that Mr. Kalo notify
Sheriff Services prior to attending to file any materials.

IV – Motion to Strike

The Defendant’s Motion

[
32
]

Mr. Kalo made a motion to strike the within
matter on the basis that it has already been heard and dismissed
ex parte
by
a judicial justice of the peace of the Provincial Court of Manitoba. To this
end, he filed a printout from the Court’s registry showing the applicant applied
for a protection order on November 21, 2025, and it was dismissed the same day.
Mr. Kalo argued the applicant applied for the protection order on the same grounds
as the present peace bond application, though no materials were filed in this
regard. He argued that allowing the applicant to proceed to seek a peace bond
against him brings the administration of justice into disrepute as there should
be no allowance for relitigating a matter that has already been dismissed. Mr.
Kalo also emphasized that the protection order was dismissed by a judicial
justice of the peace through the Court of King’s Bench, while this peace bond
hearing is proceeding through the Provincial Court.

The Applicant’s Response

[
33
]

Counsel for the applicant submitted that
the legislation for a protection order is different from that of a peace bond
and argued that Mr. Kalo’s motion on this point should be dismissed.

The Law, Analysis and Decision

[
34
]

The applicant has applied for a peace bond
pursuant to section 810 of the
Code
, where the Court must consider
whether there are reasonable grounds for the applicant’s fear that the respondent
will cause personal injury to them, their intimate partner or child, or will
damage their property, or will publish intimate images of them without their consent.

[
35
]

A protection order application is made
under
The Domestic Violence and Stalking Act
, CCSM cD93. A judicial
justice of the peace may grant a protection order if the respondent is
committing or has committed domestic violence against the subject or is
stalking or has stalked the subject, the subject believes the respondent will
continue or resume the domestic violence or stalking, the subject requires
protection because there is a reasonable likelihood the domestic violence or
stalking will continue or resume, and the seriousness or urgency of the
circumstances means an order should be made without delay (see section 6(1)).

[
36
]

I do not know why the protection order was
dismissed. I also do not know what facts were relied on during the protection
order application or hearing. That said, even if the protection order
application set out precisely the same facts as the current matter, I am
satisfied it makes no difference. A peace bond is distinct from a protection
order: one is through federal legislation while the other is through provincial
legislation, though neither requires an offence to have taken place for an
order to be granted and both are preventative in nature. Each order has a
different legal test and offers different possible relief; a dismissal of one
is not a bar to an application for the other. As such, the current application
cannot be seen to amount to relitigating a matter already decided – the
applicant had not applied for relief under section 810 of the
Code
. That
the protection order was dismissed by a judicial justice of the peace through
the Court of King’s Bench of Manitoba speaks to how
The Domestic Violence
and Stalking Act
has been established; it does not and cannot bar an
applicant seeking a recognizance order under section 810 of the
Code
.

[
37
]

While not addressed specifically during
Mr. Kalo’s various motions before the Court, Mr. Kalo had previously indicated
he would be seeking the Court – or government – cover the costs associated with
ordering a transcript of the dismissed protection order hearing. No authority
was presented to support this request. Counsel for the applicant indicated her
office would not be taking carriage of that request and would not be ordering or
relying on a transcript from the protection order hearing, though she
acknowledged that it may be relevant and appropriate for Mr. Kalo to use in the
peace bond hearing.

[
38
]

While I appreciate that the protection
order application and hearing may be relevant to this hearing – notably on
cross-examination – this remains a separate and distinct application, with a
different legal test, from the protection order hearing. The Court would rarely
wade into considering whether to order transcripts or materials on behalf of a
defendant, especially on a separate and distinct matter, and this would seem to
be especially the case in a hearing for a peace bond under section 810 of the
Code

– a hearing that often takes place with self-represented litigants on both
sides. I have not and am not at this time making an order that the Court procure
a transcript of the protection order hearing or a copy of the application filed
in support of the protection order application.

V – Motion to Replace Courtroom Security

The Defendant’s Motion

[
39
]

Mr. Kalo told the Court that he is
intimidated by the applicant’s colleagues who provide security in the
courtroom. He requested members of Protective Services, private police officers,
or supervisors to the sheriffs as replacements. When asked about the Court’s
authority to make such an order, Mr. Kalo responded that not everything
requires authority.

The Applicant’s Response

[
40
]

Counsel for the applicant indicated that
the test for replacing the sheriffs in the courtroom is whether the
administration of justice is brought to disrepute by their presence. She said
that there is no one better at protection than the Court’s sheriffs and noted
that Mr. Kalo’s erratic behaviour through the proceedings necessitates their
presence.

The Law, Analysis and Decision

[
41
]

The Provincial Court Act
clarifies
that I have “jurisdiction throughout Manitoba to exercise the powers and
perform the duties conferred or imposed on justices of the peace by or under
provincial or federal Acts:” see section 47. It also sets out that “[e]very
judge and justice of the peace has the same power and authority to preserve
order in the court in which he or she presides as may be exercised by a judge
of the Court of King’s Bench”: see section 70.

[
42
]

Trial judges have discretion to decide on
issues of courtroom security, though this typically relates to questions of
shackling and handcuffing, and general court security measures have been upheld
under the superior court’s inherent jurisdiction:
see
R v Lindsay
,

1999 CanLII 14150 (MB QB)
,
[1999] 137 Man R (2d) 68 (MBQB)
at paragraphs
32-33 and 42
.

[
43
]

I am not satisfied that my power to
preserve order in the courtroom in the present circumstances extends to allowing
me to order the presence of private security. While I appreciate that the
sheriffs at the Winnipeg Law Courts Building are colleagues to the applicant,
there has been nothing presented to suggest that this has affected how Mr. Kalo
has been treated, though his regular outbursts in the proceedings have
underlined the importance of courtroom security. Given this, I am also not
satisfied there is a need for replacement security, should I have such a power.

[
44
]

While Mr. Kalo stated that he was
intimidated by the sheriff in the courtroom, who is a colleague of the
applicant, he persistently engaged with the sheriff in the courtroom throughout
the proceeding. At no time did Mr. Kalo appear to be intimidated. Mr. Kalo was
persistent in his insults, outlandish claims, and sexual comments, and he
regularly interrupted whomever was speaking and rarely heeded warnings from the
Court. Nothing about Mr. Kalo’s conduct suggested it was in any way curtailed
by the presence of a sheriff in the courtroom.

VI – Motion to Bring a Service Animal

The Defendant’s Motion

[
45
]

Mr. Kalo requested bringing his dog,
Bator, to the next day of the proceedings. He advised the dog is mid-sized and
helps him stay calm. He advised the government could provide a dog – but he
would like a service animal for the proceedings. He said anything can be a
service animal and there is nothing regulating service animals in Manitoba.
When asked if the dog has any training, Mr. Kalo indicated he trained the
animal himself. He also indicated he has a permanent and severe disability and
takes medication for anxiety. He denied having a prescription of any sort for a
service animal.

The Applicant’s Response

[
46
]

Counsel for the applicant took no position
on the motion but noted the importance of everyone in the courtroom feeling
safe and the animal not being unruly.

The Law, Analysis and Decision

[
47
]

The evidentiary record for this motion was
lacking. Despite this, given Mr. Kalo indicated he is on disability, from which
I take it to mean that he is a person with a disability, and he indicated that
his dog Bator assists him and has been trained, albeit self-trained, for that
purpose, I approved that Bator may attend these proceedings. In doing so I am treating
Bator as a service animal as defined by
The Service Animal Protection Act
,
CCSM cS90, and
The Human Rights Code
, CCSM cH175. I also rely on my
discretion to manage conduct of matters in my courtroom, which allows for
accommodations to particular individuals as deemed appropriate: see
for example

R v JLK
,
2015 BCPC 139
at

para
7
.

[
48
]

That said, typically for a motion of this
nature, one would expect far more than was provided: while Mr. Kalo is correct
that there is no official registry of service animals in Manitoba, there must
still be evidence pointing to training to assist a person with a disability in
a way that relates to the person’s disability. Evidence on this would typically
be expected to be presented to support the attendance of a service animal,
whether through a prescription or otherwise.

[
49
]

In permitting Bator to attend these
proceedings, I issued the following caveats: the animal must not be disruptive
and it must be appropriate in the courtroom at all times. I was very clear that
any behaviour that challenges those requirements will result in the animal being
removed, and that this includes any behaviour that could be seen to intimidate
any witness in the courtroom, including during cross-examination.

VII – Stay of Proceedings Pending Appeal

The Defendant’s Position

[
50
]

Mr. Kalo advised the Court that if his
recusal motion were unsuccessful, he would be seeking a “stay of proceedings
for leave to appeal to a higher court,” and emphasized that his intention would
be to appeal. No authority was cited for this position.

The Applicant’s Response

[
51
]

Counsel for the applicant did not
specifically address this aspect of Mr. Kalo’s arguments.

The Law, Analysis and Decision

[
52
]

Steele J considered the nature of criminal
appeals in
Winnipeg (City of) v The Neighbourhood Bookstore and Café Ltd
,

2019 MBCA 3
, setting out that:

[20]   An appeal court has no inherent
jurisdiction to hear appeals in criminal matters.  Appeals are a creature
of statute and, in order for this Court to take jurisdiction to hear this
motion, the jurisdiction must be found in a statute (
see
R v Deschamps
,

2003 MBCA 116
at para
27
).

…

[26]   Under section 830(1) of the
Code
, a party
may “appeal against a conviction, judgment, verdict of acquittal or verdict of
not criminally responsible on account of mental disorder or of unfit to stand
trial or other final order or determination of a summary conviction
court”.  Section 839 allows appeals to the Court of Appeal from
decisions made by the summary conviction appeal court.

[27]   Upon interpreting section 839 of the
Code
,

in
R v Scott
,
2015 MBCA 80
, this Court held that the “
Code
only
provides for appeals of
final
orders” (at para 4) (emphasis
added).  In that case, the accused was seeking to appeal a trial judge’s
interlocutory evidentiary ruling.  The Court found that the
Canadian
Charter of Rights and Freedoms

“rulings within a prosecution are
interlocutory in nature and, therefore, are not final orders” (
ibid
).
Accordingly, the Court found it did not have jurisdiction to hear the appeal.

[
53
]

As peace bonds are governed by Part XXVII
(“Summary Convictions”) under the
Code
, sections 830 and 813(a)(i) set
out how and when appeals may be made. Section 830 allows for parties to
proceedings to appeal “against a conviction, judgment, verdict of acquittal or verdict
of not criminally responsible on account of mental disorder or of unfit to
stand trial or other final order or determination of a summary conviction
court” for being erroneous on a point of law, outside of the summary conviction
court’s jurisdiction, or a refusal or failure to exercise jurisdiction. Section
813(1)(a) of the
Code
sets out that a defendant may appeal “from a
conviction or order made against him,” without limiting the reasons for the
appeal. A recognizance order, if granted, is clearly an order or final order
made against a defendant. Neither section allows for interlocutory appeals.

[
54
]

Insofar as there may be any doubt that my
decision not to recuse myself in this matter constitutes an interlocutory decision,
the Manitoba Court of Appeal has recently rejected that an appeal from a
decision denying a recusal order, despite potential impacts to substantive and
procedural rights to a fair proceeding, holding that it nevertheless amounts to
an interlocutory appeal, albeit on a civil matter: see
Johnson Mushinski v
Manitoba (Labour Board)
,
2025 MBCA 67
at paras
3
, 18-23.

[
55
]

As such, I am satisfied that my decision
on Mr. Kalo’s recusal motion is an interlocutory decision with no statutory
basis for appeal or authority for Mr. Kalo’s request for a stay of proceedings
pending an appeal of this decision; his request for the same is denied.

56
]

I have made various references throughout
this decision to Mr. Kalo’s persistently unruly, offensive, and disruptive behaviour
as the proceedings unfolded on February 3, 2026. It is no exaggeration to say

[

]

Early in the proceedings on February 3,

[

]

The Court cannot and will not tolerate contemptuous

…I can
appreciate that for an accused person courtroom proceedings are [often] very
stressful, they are tense, they may be frustrating, but there is a certain

(See
R
v Fizell
, 2001 MBPC CanLII 14844 (MBPC) at para 21.)

61
]
